title: Mornings with Graham & Emmy
teaser: Lawmakers review bills that could speed or slow projects and affect your electric bill.

lines.text: Good morning, and welcome to Mornings with Graham & Emmy — the Michigan Data Wire, your podcast on Michigan's data center buildout. I'm Graham.
And I'm Emmy.
This morning we're zeroing in on Lansing as lawmakers weigh new tax breaks and power rules that could reshape how these big facilities come online across the state.
Right, Graham. The lead story today is those bills in the legislature that would change taxes and electricity access for data centers needing hundreds of megawatts.
Exactly. This isn't just paperwork. It touches electric bills, water use, farmland, and what towns actually keep in revenue.
So walk me through the history here. How did we get to this point with multiple bills floating around?

Well, data center interest has been building for a while. Yesterday we saw the state quietly broaden tax incentives that already let operators skip most local property taxes for up to 12 years in many places.
That sounds like it gives companies a big edge but leaves townships with less leverage.
Precisely. And now today's proposals could either speed projects up with more breaks or add rules on how they secure power from the grid.
Who are the main players pushing or resisting these changes?
You've got lawmakers in Lansing reviewing the packages, utilities dealing with the load, developers wanting fast approvals, and residents plus local officials worried about costs.
And the stakes for regular folks? Higher utility bills if upgrades get passed through to ratepayers?
That's the big concern. Residents across the state could see higher electric bills or, in some cases, new local revenue depending on what passes.
What about water and farmland? These places use a lot of both, right?
They do. Cooling systems pull serious water, and large sites often sit on or near farmland. Towns have to weigh that against any promised jobs or taxes.
How many communities have already hit pause because of these issues?
Quite a few. We've seen moratoriums in places like Wixom and Ypsilanti Township, plus pushback in St. Joseph County and New Buffalo.
And the Campbell coal plant staying open ties right into this power hunger, doesn't it?
It does. The DOE ordered it to keep running specifically because of rising demand from data centers, which means continued emissions and costs for western Michigan ratepayers.
So what happens next with these Lansing bills? Any timeline?
They're still in review, so expect more debate, possible amendments, and public input before anything final. The outcomes could set the pace for projects statewide.
And if they speed things up, how does that affect communities already strained on the grid?
It could accelerate load growth in places like Washtenaw County, where officials are pitching a new center as an economic win but residents are questioning the demands.
That tension between jobs and infrastructure costs keeps coming up.
It really does. The bills try to balance attracting investment with protecting ratepayers and local resources.
Any sense of which direction the legislature leans right now?
It's still fluid. Some proposals favor incentives to compete with other states, others add guardrails on power and taxes.
We'll be watching those votes closely.
Absolutely. Let's shift to some quick hits from around the state.
In Washtenaw County, leaders are highlighting jobs and tax revenue from a fresh data center proposal.
Right, while residents question the power and water demands on an already strained grid.
Taxpayers nearby would ultimately cover any utility upgrades needed.
Next, St. Joseph County is drafting a noise ordinance for 24/7 data centers.
Officials are also tracking extra power pulls from the regional grid, with residents within 30 miles worried about the constant hum and higher rates.
Over in Wixom, leaders may lift the data center freeze months early.
That could reopen the door for proposals that have already sparked pushback in Oakland County suburbs.
In New Buffalo, the township board rejected a permit for a storage yard tied to a data center project.
Residents in Berrien County now face fewer construction impacts and truck traffic.
Yesterday we learned Michigan broadened those tax breaks shielding data centers from most local property taxes for up to 12 years.
Rural counties like Big Rapids could lose millions while still bearing higher electricity and water costs.
Also yesterday, developer Raeden sued the state, claiming the moratorium illegally blocked its $500 million Gibraltar project.
The lawsuit could force compensation or lift restrictions in Wayne County.
Data center backlash has spurred recall bids against 28 Michigan officials, though only one made the November ballot.
Residents are venting frustration over projects they feel powerless to stop.
And in Ypsilanti Township, officials are weighing a temporary ban on new transmission lines for the U-M data center project.
It aims to buy time for residents worried about rate hikes and farmland loss in eastern Washtenaw County.
Now let's look at what's on deck for listeners who want to weigh in.
Today the Waterford Township Planning Commission meets on a six-month extension of its data center moratorium.
Springfield Township Board has a data center ordinance discussion on the agenda.
The Council on Climate Solutions is taking up data centers and environmental review.
Springfield Township Planning Commission also reviews the ordinance and zoning regulations.
And the Ann Arbor City Planning Commission has a presentation on local impacts, policy context, and zoning for Michigan communities.
Plenty of chances to show up and be heard.
Full sources and the live map at the Michigan Data Center Tracker.
We're back tomorrow.

episode_title: Lansing Weighs Tax Breaks and Power Rules for Data Centers
